title: Multipronged approach to characterize the promiscuity and mechanism of PACE transporters
text:
The Proteobacterial Antiseptic Efflux (PACE) family of transporters are a major contributor to chlorhexidine
resistance. This family was only discovered about 10 years ago, and the structure, transport mechanism and
full substrate profile are not yet known. This proposal combines structural biology, in vitro transport assays and
functional studies in bacteria to address these gaps in knowledge.

title: Understudied rare disease genes that cause heterotaxy in zebrafish
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because we will develop new tools to study genes implicated
in rare diseases that have not been studied to date. These tools will enable future research into deeper studies
on gene function and support drug screening efforts aimed at identifying compounds that can modulate these
candidate proteins in therapeutic strategies. Thus, this proposed work aligns with the NIH’s mission to develop
the fundamental knowledge needed to promote longer, healthier lives and reduce the burden of disease.

title: Decoding Nuclear Mechanosignaling and Epigenetic Mediators of Mechanical Memory in Cardiomyocytes
text:
The nucleus serves as the cells control center of forces and responds by regulating transcription that drives
changes in cell fate. How cardiomyocytes nuclear signaling is affected by temporary physical forces is poorly
understood, yet growing evidence suggests that aberrant chromatin and phenotypic changes persist despite the
ceasing of the physical forces which might lead to long-term heart issues. This proposal aims to clarify how
progression of diseased cardiomyocytes in the heart changes over time and whether it can be reversed by
examining permanent DNA, epigenetic, structural, and functional changes in the myocardium and provide ways
to help restore the heart’s health by reversing these load dependent persistent changes.

title: Investigation of ecDNA as a Driver of Intratumoral Heterogeneity and Treatment Resistance in High-Risk Medulloblastoma
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health as it focuses on extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA), which is
frequently observed in particularly aggressive cancers. These studies will improve our understanding of the
molecular mechanisms that drive tumor heterogeneity and treatment resistance in some of the most difficult-to-
treat medulloblastoma patients. Thus, the proposed research is relevant to the part of the NIH’s mission that
pertains to the causes, prevention, and cure of human diseases.

title: Population Research Core
text: PROJECT SUMMARY – Population Research Shared Resource The mission of the newly proposed USC Norris Comprehensive Cancer Center (NCCC) Population Research Shared Resource (PRC) is to maximize the impact of NCCC's research on priority cancer burdens and disparities in the catchment area and beyond, by consultation and coordinated access to unique local and national population-based data resources and assessment tools. The NCCC strategic planning process and 2018 annual core survey identified member needs for a state-of-the-art Shared Resource (SR) to provide consultation, access, and support for leveraging population-based data resources. To respond to this need, NCCC created PRC in February 2019, overseen by NCCC Administration and led by Myles Cockburn PhD, recruited to NCCC and appointed Director of PRC. As PRC Director, Cockburn advertises to and ensures access by NCCC members; oversees and evaluates the effectiveness, timeliness, and impact of PRC services; and ensures integration with other NCCC SRs. Key services provided by PRC this grant cycle include: 1) surveillance study consultation and access to data on catchment area cancer burdens; 2) geospatial linkage and analysis to assess recruitment feasibility, target interventions, and monitor intervention effects at individual/neighborhood level; 3) access to and interpretation of medical claims data (in SEER Medicare) and California's prescription and hospital discharge data (linked to LA CSP); and 4) consultation on collection, preparation, and analysis of novel individual- level naturalistic data (ecological momentary assessment (EMA), accelerometry and UV dosimetry). In response to feedback from NCCC members and aligned with the NCCC Strategic Plan, in the next grant cycle, PRC will run training sessions for clinical investigators on the use of EMA and other technologies in clinical research studies, including studies to improve survivorship (i.e., physical activity, reducing obesity, and assessing mood). Since its inception in 2019, 33 NCCC members in Cancer Control Research (CCR), Cancer Epidemiology (CE) and Translational and Clinical Sciences (TACS) research programs utilized PRC with 60 publications resulting from PRC engagement. PRC also contributed to 19 grant submissions resulting in five newly funded grants totaling $1.8M in direct costs including three NCI R01 grants and two funded CCSG P30 supplements. The anticipated annual budget of PRC in the first year of the next grant cycle is $435,646, yet the CCSG request is $108,485. Accordingly, PRC leverages extensive institutional and recharge support and seeks only 25% from CCSG funds.

title: Mechanisms of Platelet Activity in Vascular Disease
text:
Peripheral artery disease (PAD) represent a major cause of cardiac and limb morbidity and all-cause
mortality in Western society. Emerging data from our group indicate the importance of platelet activity
and platelet's non-hemostatic role in the regulation of PAD, yet this is an understudied area. Our work
aims to fill this void by investigating the role of platelets in PAD and other phenotypes of vascular
disease, and the molecular mechanisms by which coding and noncoding RNAs regulate platelet
activity and influence the pathogenesis of PAD and its consequences, with the ultimate goal of
identifying novel prognostic/diagnostic approaches and therapeutic targets for the treatment and
prevention of vascular disease.

title: Delivery of GPNMB Therapeutics for Bone Regeneration
text:
Challenges with autogenous bone grafts have prompted significant need for effective and safe
alternatives. We propose to develop and evaluate Gpnmb-therapeutics delivered via
thermoresponsive hydrogels as an innovative therapeutic strategy for bone regeneration.

title: Defining the Role of TCF21 in Adventitial Fibroblasts in Atherosclerosis
text:
Adventitial fibroblasts are a population of cells that undergo marked changes in behavior upon the development
of coronary artery disease. TCF21 is a transcription factor associated with coronary artery disease, and we
suspect that TCF21 controls adventitial fibroblasts to protect against atherosclerosis. To investigate this, we will
significantly increase the level of TCF21 in adventitial fibroblasts and examine how this changes the degree of
atherosclerosis, and utilize genetic tools to understand how higher levels of TCF21 affect adventitial fibroblasts
as well as other cells that contribute to plaque.

title: Neural Mitochondria and Gene Editing
text:
Mitochondria are regarded as critical components inside of brain cells and crucial for normal brain cell function.
This project uses new gene editing technology to study mitochondria in human brain cells.

title: Unraveling the Mechanisms of Neoantigen Vaccine-Induced Epitope Spreading
text:
Neoantigen vaccines represent an emerging class of immunotherapy, as they can effectively induce and amplify
anti-tumor T cell responses. While in the past, the phenomenon of epitope spreading has been linked to improved
clinical outcome, it has not yet been studied at scale due to technical challenges. In these studies, I propose to
systematically dissect neoantigen vaccine-induced epitope spreading by applying cutting edge immunogenomics
tools.

title: Chemical language models for peptide engineering
text:
Large language models are becoming increasingly important for research into and engineering of both proteins
and small molecules. However, there are currently no good models for peptides, which are larger than small
molecules but smaller than typical proteins. This project will develop such models and validate them
experimentally. This research will unlock important application areas in the engineering of cyclic peptides and
peptides with modified or non-standard amino acids.

title: Proteomics and model organism humanization to decode human genetics
text:
Deeply conserved human genes are strongly linked to diverse diseases, from cancer to neurodegeneration to
cardiovascular disease. We propose to study these critical human genes by (1) using a comparative proteomics
approach to biochemically define how the encoded proteins physically organize into multiprotein assemblies,
which will help us better understand a variety of human genetic diseases, (2) systematically replacing yeast
genes with their human equivalents, using the humanized yeast to directly experimentally measure the effects
of human genetic variation and gene-drug interactions, and (3) advancing new proteomics technologies that
would have broad applications across biology and medicine. Success of these efforts will provide new insights
into basic human cell biology and biochemistry, laying the foundation for future attempts to intervene, chemically
or genetically, with proteins critical to human cell health and disease.

title: The role of subsynaptic nanoscale architecture in inhibitory synaptic plasticity
text:
GABAergic inhibitory synapses mediate synaptic inhibition in the brain by regulating neuronal excitability, cell
firing, dendritic integration, and synaptic plasticity – mechanisms which are critical for learning, memory, and
cognition, and are disrupted in disease. The goal of this project is to investigate the fine details of synapse
organization to understand how nanoscale subsynaptic architecture contributes to functional synaptic plasticity.
This will begin to identify molecular interactions and structural mechanisms involved in the function and plasticity
of inhibitory synapses and offer clues to how they are disrupted during disease.

title: A universal toolkit for single-cell somatic mutation detection and its application to aging-related processes
text:
Somatic mutations accumulate in every nucleated cell in the human body during aging, affecting aging and
aging-related degeneration, but can only be studied with recently developed single cell and single molecule
sequencing technologies. Bioinformatic tools to analyze data from these technologies are not unified—i.e., they
only detect certain subtypes of mutations, apply only to specific technologies, do not encompass analysis of
data quality and are not designed to integrate other single-cell data modalities such as single cell RNA-seq. I
aim to develop a comprehensive single-cell toolkit for soup-to-nuts analysis of the leading single cell
technologies and will apply it to characterize the clonal architecture of healthy human brain and to catalog
aging-associated somatic mutations in a massive, multi-tissue dataset from the SMaHT Network.

title: Engineering cell type-specific splicing regulation
text:
This research seeks to develop predictive and cell type-specific models of alternative splicing by learning from
millions of synthetic splicing constructs, characterized across a large number of cell types. Models will be
combined with molecular design algorithms to engineer splicing constructs that target protein production to
cells of interest thus providing a path toward increasing the specificity of future gene therapies.

title: Developing a microfluidic human neurovascular unit system to investigate genetic and age-related risk factors in Alzheimer's disease
text:
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with severe impairment of
memory, cognition and executive functions that has a tremendous health and economic burden as more people
live longer. Neurovascular unit (NVU) damage, blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction and extracellular matrix
(ECM) disruption play a key etiological role in AD progression; yet the contribution of genetic and/or
environmental risk factors for brain vascular pathology is unclear. This project will establish protocols to generate
validated human pluripotent stem cells (PSC)-derived NVU cells, develop a perfused microphysiological 3D NVU
system with plasma or blood from young or aged patients and compare it transcriptome changes in human AD
brain vasculome to facilitate discovery of novel pathogenic mechanisms driving disease and evaluate the efficacy
of potential therapeutics that target the NVU in AD in future studies.

title: Fundamentals of Anti-Sickling Therapies
text:
Sickle cell disease afflicts 100,000 Americans and millions world-wide, and recently has
seen new hope in gene therapies and drug discovery. This work will provide essential
fundamental information that underlies these breakthroughs to allow them to reach their
full potential, by optimizing their effectiveness and thus improving countless lives.

title: Impact of TNF on Oncolytic Virotherapy
text:
The anti-tumor immunity induced by oncolytic virotherapy is blunted by numerous poorly characterized cellular
pathways. For example, our preliminary data demonstrates the presence of TNF within the tumor
microenvironment prevents effective oncolytic therapy by directly killing anti-tumor T cells. The current
proposal will more fully examine the impact of TNF on oncolytic therapy by understanding the molecular
mechanisms involved and identifying how to best translate these findings into human patients.

title: Cellular Systems Genetic Approaches to Understanding Regulatory Variation
text:
Our bodies originate from the genetically controlled program of differentiation encoded in our DNA, starting from
a single cell at fertilization. Variations in DNA sequences between individuals within a population can influence
normal health and disease susceptibility by altering the regulation of genome organization and function during
development. The goal of this proposal is to determine the molecular mechanisms by which this DNA sequence
variation impacts cellular identity, cell fate, and developmental outcomes.

title: Regenerate the lung through a better understanding of development
text:
Despite the recent advances in pulmonary medicine, still little is known about how posttranscriptional
modification regulates lung development, regeneration and recovery. This proposal will explore the mechanisms
by which posttranscriptional modification controls the specification and differentiation of lung progenitor cells
during lung development, injury-repair and reprogramming. This knowledge will offer insights about disease
mechanisms and can inform about potential new treatments.
